lessons.title: Gas exchange surfaces
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Exchange surfaces; transport in animals and plants (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the link between surface area to volume ratio and the need for exchange surfaces.
Describe gas exchange in fish, insects and humans.
Calculate surface area to volume ratios and pulmonary ventilation.
reviewNotes: Typical values for adult tidal volume at rest (about 500 cm³) are approximate teaching values.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Why exchange surfaces are needed
blocks.md: As an organism gets larger, its **surface area : volume ratio** falls, so diffusion across the body surface alone cannot supply enough oxygen. Large active organisms have specialised **exchange surfaces** with a large surface area, a thin barrier (short diffusion pathway) and a steep concentration gradient, kept steep by ventilation and blood flow (**Fick's law**: rate ∝ area × gradient ÷ thickness).

blocks.title: Surface area : volume
blocks.md: Do not say a bigger organism has less surface area; it has **more** area in total but **less area per unit volume**. For a cube of side s: surface area = 6s², volume = s³, so the ratio is 6 ÷ s. Doubling the side halves the ratio. Fish gills work because water and blood flow in **opposite directions** (counter-current); a parallel flow would equalise concentrations half-way along.

blocks.caption: Surface area : volume ratio falls as a cube gets larger.
blocks.alt: Three bars for cubes of side 1, 2 and 4 cm with ratios 6, 3 and 1.5.

blocks.title: Gas exchange in three groups
blocks.md:
- **Fish**: gill filaments covered in lamellae; counter-current flow; the operculum pumps water over the gills.
- **Insects**: air enters spiracles and travels down tracheae to tracheoles; muscle movements ventilate; no blood transport of oxygen.
- **Humans**: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli; alveolar epithelium one cell thick, surrounded by capillaries; surfactant lowers surface tension.

blocks.title: Breathing and lung volumes
blocks.md: **Inspiration**: external intercostal muscles contract (ribs up and out), diaphragm contracts and flattens; thorax volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in. **Expiration** at rest is passive: muscles relax, elastic recoil. **Pulmonary ventilation** = tidal volume × breathing rate. A spirometer records volumes (tidal volume, vital capacity).

blocks.title: Worked example — ratio of cubes
blocks.statement: Calculate the surface area : volume ratio of cubes of side 2 cm and 4 cm.
steps: 2 cm cube: area 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; volume 8 cm³; ratio 24 ÷ 8 = 3.0.
4 cm cube: area 6 × 16 = 96 cm²; volume 64 cm³; ratio 96 ÷ 64 = 1.5.
Doubling the side halves the ratio.

blocks.title: Worked example — pulmonary ventilation
blocks.statement: A student at rest has a tidal volume of 500 cm³ and breathes 12 times per minute. Calculate the pulmonary ventilation.
steps: Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate.

lessons.title: The heart and circulation
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Exchange surfaces; transport in animals and plants (to be checked)

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the structure and double circulation of the mammalian heart.
Explain the cardiac cycle and the roles of the valves.
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries; calculate cardiac output.
reviewNotes: Heart diagram orientation (viewer's left = right side of the heart) is standard.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: A double circulatory system
blocks.md: In mammals blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: the **pulmonary circulation** (heart → lungs → heart) and the **systemic circulation** (heart → body → heart). This keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart and lets blood return to the heart for a pressure boost before travelling to the body, supporting a high metabolic rate.

blocks.title: Left and right on diagrams
blocks.md: Heart diagrams are drawn as if looking at the person facing you, so the **right** side of the heart is on **your left**. The **left ventricle** has the thicker muscle wall. Arteries carry blood *away* from the heart and veins carry blood *towards* it; it is **not** true that arteries always carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).

blocks.caption: The four chambers of the heart and the double circulation.
blocks.alt: Four boxes for the atria and ventricles with arrows to and from the body and lungs.

blocks.title: The cardiac cycle
blocks.md:
1. **Atrial systole**: atria contract; blood pushed into ventricles.
2. **Ventricular systole**: ventricles contract; atrioventricular valves close (first sound), semilunar valves open; blood leaves by aorta and pulmonary artery.
3. **Diastole**: heart relaxes; semilunar valves close (second sound); atria fill.
The **sinoatrial node** (the pacemaker) starts each beat.

blocks.title: Blood vessels and output
blocks.md:
- **Arteries**: thick elastic and muscular walls, narrow lumen, high pressure.
- **Veins**: thin walls, wide lumen, valves, low pressure.
- **Capillaries**: one-cell-thick wall, huge total surface area.
**Cardiac output** = stroke volume × heart rate. Tissue fluid forms at the arterial end of capillaries by high hydrostatic pressure; most returns at the venous end by osmosis and the rest by the lymph.

blocks.title: Worked example — cardiac output
blocks.statement: A resting man has a stroke volume of 70 cm³ and a heart rate of 72 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output.
steps: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
= 5040 cm³ per minute (about 5 dm³ per minute).

blocks.title: Worked example — pressure and valves
blocks.statement: In the cardiac cycle the pressure in the left ventricle rises above the pressure in the left atrium. State what happens to the valves and why this matters.
steps: Higher pressure in the ventricle pushes the atrioventricular valve shut.
This prevents blood from flowing backwards into the atrium.
When ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the semilunar valve opens and blood leaves.
blocks.answer: AV valve closes; semilunar valve opens

objectives: Describe the structure of xylem and phloem.
Explain the cohesion-tension theory and the factors affecting transpiration.
Describe mass flow in phloem and calculate water uptake from a potometer.
reviewNotes: Mass-flow and cohesion-tension are presented as accepted models; the details of loading mechanisms may exceed the syllabus.
Potometer volume uses V = πr²d; teachers should check units.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Transpiration stream
blocks.md: **Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the leaves, mainly through the **stomata**. Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls, lowering the water potential in the leaf and **pulling** water up the **xylem**. Water molecules stick together (**cohesion**) and to the vessel walls (**adhesion**), so the column does not break. This is the **cohesion-tension theory**. Water enters roots by osmosis down a water-potential gradient.

blocks.title: Xylem is not powered by living cells
blocks.md: Xylem vessels are dead, so water movement in them is **passive**. Do not say that xylem pumps water by active transport. **Root pressure** (from active salt uptake into the xylem) contributes a little but cannot lift water to the top of tall trees. Transpiration is a result of gas exchange: stomata must open to let CO₂ in, and water inevitably escapes.

items.text: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis
Crosses the cortex to the xylem
Evaporates from mesophyll cells in the leaf

blocks.caption: Water travels from the soil to the atmosphere in the transpiration stream.
blocks.alt: Five boxes in a vertical chain from root hair cells through the xylem to the stomata.

blocks.title: Factors affecting transpiration
blocks.md: Rate increases with **light** (stomata open), **temperature** (more evaporation), **wind** (removes humid air), and decreases with **humidity**. Xerophytes have adaptations such as thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled leaves and hairs. A **potometer** measures water uptake: volume = πr² × distance moved by the air bubble.

blocks.title: Phloem and mass flow
blocks.md: **Phloem** has living **sieve tube elements** (with perforated sieve plates) and **companion cells**. Sucrose is loaded actively into sieve tubes at the **source** (e.g. leaves), lowering water potential so water enters by osmosis. Pressure rises and sap flows to the **sink** (roots, fruits, growing points) where sucrose is removed. This is the **mass flow** hypothesis.

blocks.title: Worked example — potometer
blocks.statement: In a potometer the air bubble moves 45 mm in 5 minutes. The capillary tube has radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the volume of water taken up and the rate.

blocks.title: Worked example — predicting a change
blocks.statement: A leafy shoot is moved from a still, humid room in Buea to a sunny, windy balcony. Predict and explain the change in water uptake.
steps: Wind removes humid air near the stomata, steepening the water-potential gradient.
Light opens the stomata and heat increases evaporation.
So transpiration and water uptake both increase.
